title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 7: Chao-chou: "Wash Your Bowl"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 7 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Zhaozhou answers a new monk's request for teaching by asking if he has eaten his morning gruel, then telling him to wash his bowl. Nomon compares translations of the monk's final realization, reads the exchange literally as full attention to eating and washing in the oryoki meal, and notes that "just" begins the word "justice." Two recent deaths follow: Nancy Welch, whose cremation ceremony Nomon describes, and seventeen-year-old Butch Mullins, struck on I-5, which raises the mind's hunger for the full story. Nomon ends with news of a lay entrustment and a jukai cohort, and the hope that you have washed your bowl.

sentences.text: Well, the seventh story in the Mumon-Kan collection, The Barrier That Has No Gate, is a really favorite of mine.

It features Master Zhaozhou, whom we met at the beginning, the famous teacher who, when the eager young student asked him about dogs and Buddha nature, said mysteriously and weirdly, "No," or "mu" in Sino-Japanese, which then led to generations of Zen students sitting there on their cushions, and to some benefit too, strangely enough.
So anyway, here's Zhaozhou again.
Similar thing: a monk asks a question and the teacher answers not in the way the student expected.

One hopes with the intention of helping the student see a broader way of understanding, a different way of being, and then the habit-driven, performance-based, "I want to get it right" way that we tend to go about things.
*A monk said to Zhaozhou, "I've just entered your monastery, please teach me."
And Zhaozhou replied, "Have you eaten your morning rice gruel?"
The monk said, "Yes, I have."
Zhaozhou said, "Then you'd better wash your bowl."
The monk deeply understood.*
So this last line though is sort of like the outcome, that's what we want to know about: what did you get out of it?
And I've noticed, comparing different translations, there are many different ways that last line is expressed.
What does the monk understand or realize?
Some say, like I just read, the monk understood.
Others say the monk gained insight.
Some say the monk was enlightened.
There are four characters in Chinese in that last sentence.
It seems like a pretty straightforward sentence, as best as Google Translate and I can tell.
The first three characters definitely seem to say "thus monk gained."
So the monk got something.
The fourth character would seem like the crux of the matter.
It's pronounced something like "shun" or "shun."
And the first dictionary definition of this word, whatever this is, the monk gained, is actually like a province, like a county.
So the monk gained maybe some sense of territory, the territory of awakening or seeing something differently.
And then that character paired with another character means, next definition down, to save or to economize.
So that kind of works.
We do emphasize a certain kind of clarity and efficiency and economy of expression.
These wordy Dharma talks notwithstanding, right, we mostly are in silence, communicating with gesture, being very upright, very economical in our lives.
So that works.
But the last definition down in the dictionary anyway was "to examine yourself."
So maybe the monk gained some quality of self-understanding or self-examination from this exchange with a teacher, where he showed up asking for something: please teach me.
I wonder what he thought he could be taught.
And Zhaozhou started talking about the daily routine.
Have you eaten?
Please wash your bowl.

Maybe the monk in this exchange was released in some way from some kind of desire, some kind of striving for some sort of thing called teachings that he thought he was lacking, that he thought he could get.
Maybe because he himself felt lacking and wanted to get some new way of being.
So this is a wonderful story because I think we can look at it in a very literal, everyday way.
There are many layers to all these stories, but I think it's a mistake to miss the everyday ordinary interpretation, straight up.
That's the economy part, to be straight up.
So, to attend fully to what we're doing.
The teachings are right in front of you, dear monk.
Eat your cereal.
Really eat your cereal.
With full attention, with reverence.
Before eating the gruel in the oryoki meal ritual we hold up our bowls and we express the hope that eating this meal will save all beings.
We say that and we're just reading it off the card, but maybe we actually mean it.
I hope so.
What a blessing.
What a blessing to receive food and to eat, to really eat.
Maybe in that moment we wake up a little bit.
We're in awe of the richness and complexity of the flavors, the textures, the feeling of chewing.
This amazing thing that happens in our bodies as we metabolize this other substance and make it into ourselves.
It's incredible.
Eating is truly incredible if we think about it for even a minute.
Perfect.
What a blessing.
And then in our ritual the servers come in with the hot water so we can wash our bowls after that.

I was thinking what a shame it would be to think that the taste of the cereal is the important part and the rest is just ritual or just practical: now that we're awakened from our rice gruel, we've got a dirty bowl, so we better deal with that next.
Can we see that in just the same way, with just the same depth of meaning and feeling?
It's amazing to swirl out the bowl with our little scraper, our little setsu, to take care of Buddha's bowls.
That everything is a teaching.
So in a way this story, which sounds pretty practical, you just arrive somewhere, you would like some help.
But how silly to ask for teachings.
The teachings are being offered to us all the time.
The teachings are right here.
In Zen we love the English word "just."
I don't know how these things were expressed in Japanese or Chinese.
But we say: when you eat, just eat.
When you walk, just walk.
When you listen, just listen.
When you breathe, just breathe.
And this I think is really deep.
Not to be underestimated by our busy brain that wants new teachings from the teacher.
Just be.
Just be yourself.
I think we should all continue this practice of just doing exactly what we're doing and stop getting so ahead of ourselves.
How easily we zoom out of our experience into some big story, a judgment, an opinion, a desire, a fear.
That deep fear of not being good enough.
That fear that triggers us to be so needy or so aggressive or so blaming or blameworthy.
Can we drop it all?
And just be.
Unless we get worried that this is just sort of a withdrawal or a kind of navel-gazing thing, it occurred to me that "just," J-U-S-T, is also the first four letters in the word "justice."

So don't you think a grounded life lived in a deep relationship to what's happening moment after moment is the platform that we need to show up and try to advocate for change in the world, however that looks for each of us depending on our circumstances?
So just being and just breathing and just eating is not an avoidance of something.
It's the basis by which we meet the world with a little more wisdom, I hope, a little more strength and a lot more compassion.
So just eat your gruel.
Just wash your bowls.
Just come to the Zendo on Wednesday night.
Just show up.
This is the life of Bodhisattvas.
So on Sunday we had a deep opportunity to practice this.
I think about eight of us went to say goodbye to Nancy Welch's body.

We practiced just bowing, just chanting, just making offerings, being there as fully as we could with our whole hearts, and then with the help of the funeral director, Connie, with Karen's support, just pressing the button to turn on the giant oven and invite Nancy's body to transform into ash.
And now it's just ash.

And hopefully by Saturday this vast complicated thing we call a body, Nancy's body, will be in this new form in a little box on the altar and we'll do more ceremonies, just showing up for a dear friend.
But we couldn't all be there.
It was a really small place.
It wasn't set up for rituals or anything like that.
It was basically a grotty old kind of warehouse.
And there was the oven, a huge oven.
It was like these two rows together was the oven.
And then there was just room here for the body and just about this much space for the eight of us in the wall.
So I set my bowing mat here and I could just barely, just barely bow.
We offered incense, adding our own smoke to the smoke that was soon to come.
So I thought you might appreciate hearing a few statements from the ceremony since we couldn't all be there.
And if you never knew Nancy Welch, that's okay, because we are all just bound for this, right?
At one point I said:
*Nancy, we've recited the ten sacred names to nourish your spirit deeply, intending that the radiance of the jewel mirror comes forth.
May the Dharma winds reach everywhere.

We lovingly send this flower to the field of enlightenment, offering incense and chanting the Enmei Jukku Kanan Gyo, calling forth the compassion of Kanan Bodhisattva who hears the cries of the world.*
And we did, we chanted the Enmei Jukku Kanan Gyo like we just did.
Which Nancy was fond of, actually, so I was happy that was in the ritual.
And then after Connie and Karen pushed the button and the oven started roaring to life, so loud, really loud, I shouted what I assume is a traditional shout.
It probably sounds a little better in Japanese.
But I shouted, "Now fire, heat up, complete this existence."
And as the ovens roared we kept chanting and bowing.
We chanted the Heart Sutra.
And Talus, Ezra Kokyo, managed to bring forward his strong voice.
You've ever heard of Ezra Kokyo?
Very strong voice.
He was the guy for the job.
He chanted for us at the end:
*We offer the merit of our chanting to you, Yuzon G.E.
Nancy Welch, dear friend, returning to your origin.
We pray that wherever you are, your world may be beautiful.*
So beautiful.
So this practice of "just" is really woven through our whole practice in every way, our understanding.
And it helps us in so many ways.
I think we don't talk enough about this.
Because of course our minds want steps and reasons and answers and projects and solutions to our problems.

But once Dogen established his monastery, Eiheiji, and he turned his focus more fully towards training monastics, he really focused on this quality of the justness or the vastness of the Dharma, the completeness of the Dharma in and of itself.
Without needing explanations, without needing to answer our own busy mind or answer the monk who comes into the front door and wants teachings: the completeness of being.
So the tradition, the custom for his talks at Eiheiji, which must be what he saw in China, was a little different from this, actually.
The talks were much shorter and the teacher mounted a kind of high platform up above everybody a little bit.
And the monks would all stand.
We believe there were a few nuns there too, so excuse me for using mostly the male terminology.
It was mostly men, but we believe there were some nuns there too.
And the talks were really short.
And often they didn't explain a thing.
So here's a great example.
He said, and I think about year 1240, in one of these short talks, the following:
*Today this mountain monk, meaning himself, gives a dharmahal discourse.
As this discourse is given, all Buddhas in the three times also today give a dharmahal discourse.
The ancestral teachers in all generations today give a dharmahal discourse.
The one who bears a sixteen-foot golden body gives the dharmahal discourse.
The one endowed with the wondrous function of the hundred grasses gives a dharmahal discourse.
Already having given a dharmahal discourse, what dharma has been expounded?
No other dharma is expressed, but this very dharma is expressed.
What is this dharma?
It is upheld within Xianglong temple.
It is upheld within Guanyin temple.
It is upheld within the monk's hall.
It is upheld within the dharmahal, within the Buddha hall.
End.*
So imagine yourself there.
Maybe you'd be brave enough or desiring enough to raise your hand and say, "Excuse me, master, what was this dharma that was expressed?
I missed it."
Maybe Dogen would look down at you.
We don't really know what any of these people were really like, but he seemed to have been a fairly intense guy.
That comes through.
Maybe he would have looked down at you and would say to you, "You, have you eaten today?"
"Yes, master."
"Please go wash your bowl."
Maybe you would be enlightened or maybe confused.
And Dogen was a big fan of Jiaojiao.
He had certain teachers that he praised and a lot of teachers he criticized.
So he called Jiaojiao an old Buddha, which was high praise from him.

And I didn't look it up to be sure, but I believe where he talks about the different temples that he mentioned, Guanyin temple was the name of Jiaojiao's temple, so I think he was referring probably to Jiaojiao.
Some 400 years before him.
All of this a thousand years before us.
So we face the whole thing every day, don't we?
We don't know what the answers are.
We don't even know if there are answers.
And what we're really facing is life and death, and we don't understand that either.
So Nancy died a week ago, early on Monday morning, and early on this Monday morning another death happened in my life.
Not as close to me, but in a way really more difficult.
One of Walker's friends, not a close friend, but somebody Walker's known since preschool.
A classmate.
A 17-year-old boy named Butch Mullins was for some reason walking on the right lane of I-5 northbound from Meridian and was struck and killed by a car at 12:30 a.m.
The car left the scene and the whole thing is under investigation by the police.
They don't know what happened.
And it's interesting how much the mind wants to know the story.
I noticed that really strongly after getting the call initially from John Wiley early last Monday morning that Nancy was gone, but we didn't talk really.
He was just giving me the news.
When I talked to Nancy's dear friend Susan Thurn, who's been the one in charge of winding things down for her, true bodhisattva, Susan Thurn, amazing, you'll see her on Saturday if you come.
Anyway, when I called Susan an hour or so later and she told me the story of Nancy's last hour, I noticed how much I wanted to know that story.
How much I wanted to know what happened, and did she suffer?
And it was just somehow a relief.
Is that interesting?
We just want to know the stories.
Even though we know very well the story is not complete, the story will never be complete.
So I want to know the story of Butch.
He was a big guy, a big kid.
He came to a couple of Walker's birthday parties.
I didn't know him well, but he seemed to be always smiling and sweet.
And to imagine him in the middle of the night walking down the exit and onto the freeway.
Maybe no cars were in sight at that hour and just start walking along in the right lane, knowing what would happen.
But we'll probably never know what happened for him.
Death is so hard, you know?
So hard.
But maybe it's our greatest teacher, too.
Maybe that's what Jiaojiao was trying to communicate to the monk.
Death is certain.
Please pay attention.

And many of these deaths are teaching me something, or you something, or all of us something about knowing and not knowing and humility, and how central and urgent it is to really be alive while we're alive, and how important our vows and our work are.
So I've known Nancy for 26 years.
I did the math, just a little hair under half my life.
And she's always been recognizably Nancy.
I always knew it was Nancy.
The way she moved, the way she looked, the way she talked.
I keep thinking of her awesome Midwestern expression.
She would say, remember this?
She would say, "Well, shucky darns."
Remember she said that all the time?
When she was frustrated but had a little perspective.
Before that it would be like a four-letter word.
Once there was a little perspective, like, "Well, shucky darns."
Isn't that annoying?
I always knew it was Nancy.
And yet she also changed a lot over the years.
Her body changed a lot with her size and shape.
Often she was different from the last time I saw her.
Her wild frizzy hair showed up in all different configurations.
But more importantly, I think, I don't know, how do we know what's more important about a person?
Her way of being changed a lot too over the years.
She always had a very deep and powerful determination in her.
She was one determined person.
And there's all kinds of stories I could tell about why I think that is, connected to her lifelong illnesses and so on.
But that's just a story.
But no question, she was determined, whatever it was she was trying to do.

But in the early years, in my memory now, and I was in the middle of all this with my own confusion, so who knows what really happened, in the early years it seemed like the determination was really mixed in with all kinds of complicated stuff.
Passion with jealousy, love with confusion and desire.
A deep desire for justice mixed with a powerful kind of white-hot rage at how fucked up things seem to be.
But little by little that changed.
The determination didn't, it was always still there.
But my sense was over the last years, somehow her passion just distilled and purified, and it collects sort of clarity and kindness.
I'll say more on Saturday about how important she was to me, to the formation of our sangha over the many years that she was very determined to be here.
But actually, I think now the real fruits of her practice ripened in her life in these last seven or eight years when she wasn't coming here in her body.
That's when her practice really somehow sort of kicked in.
So I'm always giving people, I must admit, subtle or not so subtle vibes that they should come here all the time.
But it was better that she wasn't coming, I think it turned out, in the end, the last years.
Somehow she turned her practice into her life in a way that didn't depend on all this formal Zen frou frau anymore.
She lived her last years as such a beautiful, wise Bodhisattva, taking care of her patients, and she was a psychotherapist, taking care of her relationship with her husband.
There were a couple of really unusual people, Nancy and John, but an incredible, wonderful, loving marriage, 25 years.
So for sure, I wish we'd had her in the world for another 26 years, but I don't get to decide that.
She doesn't get to decide that.
We don't get to decide that.
Just like I don't get to decide that Butch Mullins should be able to grow into adulthood.
That's what's supposed to happen with 17-year-old boys.
They should come forward and be beautiful men working for the world.
We don't get to decide that.
It's all such a mystery, living in this deep web of causes and effects and all of it running through birth and death and death and birth that we do not understand and will never understand.
Was that body that we slid in the oven still Nancy?
I don't think we really thought it was Nancy, but it wasn't not Nancy either.
Nancy was there, and Nancy's here now.
She'd be sitting in the back.
She'd probably be fidgeting a bit because her joints would hurt.
She'd probably be on the edge of calling something out and interrupting me.
She used to clown around a lot when Norman gave talks, which of course I was very censorious about at the time.
I'd be giving her the stink eye subtly because I'd be very upright.
We learn from each other.
But through all this mystery and all this unknowability, sometimes that expresses as confusion, sometimes it expresses as peace.
Through all of it, I really do have faith in washing our bowls.
I think it really is wise to take care of our lives, to take care of what's in front of us.
When the servers come with water, we bow.
We're so grateful.
When the news comes, we bow.
Good news, bad news.
Want a little good news?
Here's some good news.
We've got a few little scatterings of good news.
There's lots of good news, you know.
So Talus, with his strong voice, has asked me if we could work together towards lay entrustment, and I said yes.
So that'll be good, I think.
He'll start sewing the green raka suit.
I'll talk more later about what that might mean.
We're putting together a lovely little jukkui cohort this year.
It's such a wonderful process of commitment and study.
Judith will be in it.
And Wayne, there's Wayne over there.
And Ray Green.
And laughing out.
Maybe someone else will show up.
Who knows?
And other people will come to those meetings to study the precepts and support the jukkui students.
And I'm happy to get to do that with John.
Wonderful.
Lots of good things are happening.
So we're all growing and learning, and sometimes it takes 26 years of pissing each other off, but we realize how much we love each other.
And that that's what really matters.
So if you've eaten today, I hope you've washed your bowl.
That's probably enough.
Thank you.
